entry.evidence: Therefore, we implemented and tested a new inversion procedure for Rayleigh wave group velocity dispersion curves based on this method.

steps.action: Reviewed published Moho depths, slab velocities and sediment thicknesses for the Makran from seismic and gravity studies.
steps.quote: the crustal thickness under the Oman seafloor and Makran fore-arc is about 24–30 km

steps.action: Set the aim of constraining velocity and density structure of sediments, crust and upper mantle in SE Iran with a new method and new data.
steps.quote: our purpose is to constrain the seismic wave velocity variations and density structure of the sediments

steps.action: Built a Simulated Annealing inversion of fundamental-mode Rayleigh group dispersion curves for a four-layer model with linear vertical gradients, sequenced with 3D gravity inversion.
steps.quote: a Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm is applied to the nonlinear inversion of fundamental-mode Rayleigh wave group dispersion curves

steps.action: Took Rayleigh group velocity maps at 12 periods on a 1° grid from the tomography of Mohammadi et al. (2020).
steps.quote: These dispersion observations were taken from a surface wave tomographic study in the Iranian plateau

steps.action: Took global free-air gravity data from BGI and projected it onto a 0.2° grid.
steps.quote: global free-air gravity data with a resolution of 2.5 × 2.5 arc-minutes

steps.action: Computed partial derivatives of group velocity with respect to each parameter against CRUST1.0, then reduced unknowns from 28 to 20 per column (200 km model base, no sediment gradients, constant Vp/Vs, fixed LAB density).
steps.quote: We then investigated the sensitivity of the group velocities on variations of each parameter

steps.action: Tested the forward calculation for convergence with sub-layer thickness and fixed maximum sub-layer thicknesses of 3, 4 and 11 km.
steps.quote: we repeated the calculations for different numbers of sub-layers

steps.action: Inverted noise-free synthetic data 10 times, with some parameters placed near search-space bounds, and compared the result with the true model.
steps.quote: we applied this method to an arbitrary noise-free and its corresponding noisy synthetic 1D model

steps.action: Added 10 realizations of 0.1 km/s Gaussian noise, inverted each 15 times, and compared the averaged model and its standard deviation with the synthetic model.
steps.quote: we constructed 10 different data sets by adding 10 different realizations of random noise to the data

steps.action: Kept the SA procedure as working for nonlinear surface-wave inversion (relative errors mostly below 2-3%, sediments less well resolved).
steps.quote: the results from the synthetic data demonstrate that the SA method can be successfully applied

steps.action: Compared the run-to-run variability of SA with the Shuffled Complex Evolution inversion from the authors' 2018 study and judged SA more stable.
steps.quote: for the SA method, the variations of the parameter values in successive tests are small in comparison to the SCE method

steps.action: Inverted the real dispersion curves in 96 independent 1D columns, 10 runs of 100,000 iterations each, averaging the best models.
steps.quote: we applied the SA method to the real data 10 times

steps.action: Took the standard deviation across the 10 random-start runs as the parameter uncertainty (Fig. 10).
steps.quote: the standard deviation for each parameter has been calculated and is presented in Fig. 10 as an estimate of the model uncertainty

steps.action: Compared first-round data misfits (Fig. 9) with the ±0.1 km/s data uncertainty.
steps.quote: In most areas, these misfits stay within the +/-0.1 km/s uncertainty estimated by Mohammadi

steps.action: Ran a 3D linearized gravity inversion for layer thicknesses and densities, with interface depths constrained by the SA result (λ = 1, 28 iterations).
steps.quote: the density variation and thickness distribution of the different lithosphere layers were obtained

steps.action: Compared the gravity-derived thicknesses and densities (Fig. 11) with the SA model (Fig. 8) and judged the differences acceptable.
steps.quote: the thicknesses and densities have been changed slightly and in some points are somewhat different, which is acceptable

steps.action: Re-ran the SA inversion from the gravity model, with search ranges cut by 60% for densities and 10% for thicknesses and velocities, 10 runs.
steps.quote: we used the results of gravity modeling to constrain densities more than other model parameters

steps.action: Recomputed run-to-run uncertainties after the second round (Fig. 14) and found them reduced, especially for densities.
steps.quote: The resulting uncertainties were thus reduced

steps.action: Compared second-round misfits (Fig. 13) with first-round misfits and with the data uncertainty.
steps.quote: this increase is not significant and stays nearly everywhere within the estimated data uncertainties

steps.action: Checked that misfits are larger where the tomography resolution is low (east and south) and smaller inside the resolved contour.
steps.quote: as we expected, our data misfits are larger in these parts of the region

steps.action: Compared sediment thickness, Moho depths, the Minab-fault boundary and the slab velocity anomaly with published seismic studies and known geology.
steps.quote: our results are in a good agreement with the previous studies by Dolati (2010) and Kopp et al. (2000)

steps.action: Kept the final model: Moho deepening northward, crustal density decreasing northward, and high mantle velocities and densities beneath the Gulf of Oman read as the slab.
steps.quote: The Makran area is characterized by a Moho depth of about 24–30 km in the southern, oceanic part

tree.answer: Crust and upper-mantle structure of the Makran, known in outline from prior studies
No; velocities, densities and interfaces are latent and must be inverted from dispersion and gravity data
Estimate a 3D velocity-density model with a new SA-gravity sequential inversion
No rival structural hypotheses stated; only rival inversion methods (thin-layer, MCMC, SCE)
Conditions found: natural earthquake-derived dispersion data and global gravity
Synthetic noise-free and noisy tests, repeated stochastic runs, misfit within data uncertainty, agreement with prior studies
Model kept as an estimate with run-to-run uncertainties

end.claim: Moho depth across the Makran rises from 24-30 km under the Oman seafloor to 34-42 km under the forearc and 47-49 km under the Taftan-Bazman arc (uncertainty 0.1-1.6 km), with crustal density decreasing from about 2860 to 2760 kg/m3 northward.

decisive_move.sentence: The SA inversion of the real dispersion curves, refined by the gravity-constrained second SA round, produces the velocity-density-thickness model that the claim reports.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition; both data sets are taken from prior work or a public archive (pp. 4-5). The method faced synthetic tests it could have failed, and the real-data model is checked against data uncertainty and published results (pp. 9-16). No real-data claim faces a rival structural model. The synthetic models and noise level were set before inversion, but no analysis or threshold was declared in advance.

imports.item: Markov-Chain Monte Carlo as the conceptual base of SA
Shuffled Complex Evolution optimizer and its comparative assessment (Goswami and O'Connor 2007, rainfall-runoff calibration)

novelty_claims.quote: with a new method (using Simulated Annealing (SA) method) and new data as well
we implemented and tested a new inversion procedure for Rayleigh wave group velocity dispersion curves
our new surface wave data have more precision and accuracy

limits: The supplied XML text contains no body paragraphs, so every body step cites printed pages, not §-locators. The supplementary material (Tables S1-S4, Figs. S1-S6) was not supplied, so the relative errors cited from it could not be checked. No review file was supplied (the acknowledgments mention reviewers of an earlier version), so there is no review sequence. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a method demonstration on synthetic data followed by a regional estimation, with no rivals, no phenomenon to establish and no frozen forecast. Sub-claims at other statuses: the SA procedure is capability_characterized (synthetic tests, p. 10); the slab and mantle-wedge reading of the upper-mantle anomalies and the thinner lithosphere under the arc are best_explanation at most, with no rival tested (p. 16). The open question on subduction dip raised in the introduction (p. 2) is not answered. Inference: the 'new data' claim (p. 13) is supported by a citation to a hydrology paper on optimizers (Goswami and O'Connor 2007), which does not concern seismic data, so the support appears misattributed. Inference: the SCE comparison relies on the authors' 2018 study with different data, so it is not a same-data method check. The gravity inversion is constrained by the SA depths, so its agreement with the SA model is not fully independent. Uncertainties from repeated SA runs reflect search variability only, not data or parameterization uncertainty; the authors note SA gives only approximate uncertainty (p. 6). The choices of λ = 1, 5 mGal data uncertainty and the 60%/10% search-space reductions are given without sensitivity tests.

disagreements.support: The authors argue that smooth thin-layer models make geological interfaces hard to locate, and adopt a four-layer gradient parameterization instead.
disagreements.quote: it may be difficult to locate geological layer limits such as the base of a sedimentary basin or the crust-mantle boundary

disagreements.support: SA is argued to be faster because it needs fewer trial models; no timing comparison is reported.
disagreements.quote: it reduces the number of trial models and reduces thus the calculation time, the main drawback of the MCMC method

disagreements.target: Shuffled Complex Evolution inversion used in Abdollahi et al. (2018)
disagreements.support: Smaller run-to-run parameter variability of SA, shown in Fig. 7a and Tables S3-S4, set against the earlier SCE results.
disagreements.quote: the SA method can be considered more stable and therefore well suitable for the inversion of surface wave data

alternatives_considered.chosen: Four layers with linear vertical gradients in velocity and density
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Many thin constant-velocity layers (Herrmann 2013 and others)
alternatives_considered.reason: Thin-layer results give smooth transitions that make the sediment base and Moho hard to locate
SA reduces the number of trial models and so the computation time
Smaller variability of parameter values in successive tests, although SA is computationally less efficient

alternatives_considered.chosen: Only average velocity and density in sediments (no gradients)
alternatives_considered.reason: Sensitivity to sediment gradients is low or zero for thicknesses below 6 km

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Independent compressional velocity with its gradient

alternatives_considered.chosen: Maximum sub-layer thicknesses of 3 km (upper crust), 4 km (lower crust) and 11 km (mantle)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Thicker sub-layers or other numbers of sub-layers
alternatives_considered.reason: Result depends on layer number for thick sub-layers and is stable below a maximum thickness

alternatives_considered.chosen: λ = 1 in the gravity inversion cost function
alternatives_considered.reason: Small λ risks instability, large λ forces parameters to stay near initial values; λ should be as small as stability allows
